beats.text: Every coaching business runs on money it barely tracks. Card receipts in a glovebox, Stripe payouts in one tab, a bank statement nobody opens until April.
This is the AI Bookkeeper. It turns all of that into one ledger you can hand to an accountant — without you doing data entry.
Everything you're about to see is real software running on real data. Nothing here is a mockup.
Start with the ledger. Income on the left, expenses in the middle, and what's actually yours on the right.
There are three separate books. Keeping business and household money apart is the single thing accountants ask for most.
This is the spouse's business — its own books, its own totals, never mixed in.
And the household book. Personal spending lives here, which matters later when we calculate a home-office deduction.
Back to the main business book. Every number you'll see from here is scoped to whichever book is selected.
Income is the easy half, because the platform already knows about it — session packs, camps, memberships, shop orders.
Import platform income pulls straight from the money-of-record tables and drafts ledger entries for review.
It matches each payment to the right service line, so revenue is categorised before you ever look at it.
And a nightly job runs this automatically at 4:30 UTC — so new payments post themselves while you sleep.
Expenses are the hard half. This is where most bookkeeping tools ask you to type. This one doesn't.
Upload a bank or card statement — CSV or PDF — and the AI reads every row.
It proposes a category for each line, flags internal transfers so they never hit your profit and loss, and catches duplicates.
Crucially it never posts anything silently. You review, you uncheck what's wrong, and only then does it commit.
Here are the rows that came in from statements — tagged at the source, so you always know where a number came from.
A statement tells you money left. A receipt proves what it bought. The IRS cares about the difference.
Paid cash? Two taps. Amount, category, done — no photo required.
Got a paper receipt? Photograph it. Vision AI reads the vendor, the date and the total, then drops it into a review queue.
You can shoot up to fifteen at once — a whole shoebox in a single pass.
Amazon is its own special misery, so it gets its own importer that reads the order CSV directly.
And the fourth way needs no app at all.
Label a receipt email in Gmail, and an hourly job collects the attachment, scans it, and queues it here.
It's read-only against your inbox — it never marks mail read, never moves anything, never deletes.
Categories are your chart of accounts. Each one carries a tax category, so the report at the end is already in your accountant's language.
Some categories demand more. Meals, travel and vehicle require a stated business purpose — because those are the deductions that get challenged.
Write down why a lunch was a business lunch at the time, and you'll still have the answer eighteen months later.
Now the part almost every coaching business gets wrong: the difference between what clients paid and what actually landed.
Stripe takes a fee on every charge. Your gross income and your real income are not the same number.
A daily job pulls every payout and its underlying transactions, so fees are read from Stripe rather than estimated.
Gross stays the headline — that's what your accountant files on. Underneath it, the fees, and the net you actually received.
If a payout hasn't been ingested yet, this line says so plainly instead of quietly showing zero fees.
This is where it stops being a ledger and starts being a bookkeeper.
Every finding here is a candidate for your accountant to confirm — never a filed decision. That distinction is deliberate.
The deduction watchlist totals what you've spent in each deductible category, with the vendors behind it.
Substantiation gaps are the dangerous ones: money spent in a category that legally needs a stated purpose, with no purpose written down.
Uncategorized expenses can't be matched to a deduction at all. Until you categorise them, they're invisible money.
Profit by service line shows which part of the business actually makes money — camps versus team work versus one-to-one training.
Costs that don't belong to one line sit in a shared bucket. Turn on allocation and they're split by each line's share of revenue.
The vendor sweep finds recurring charges. These two are both video tools on the same category — flagged as a possible overlap you're paying twice for.
Missing receipts and purposes is the pre-audit checklist: every entry that would be hard to defend, listed in one place.
Every row here has Attach. That puts the receipt onto the entry that already exists — rather than creating a second copy of the same spend.
A rolling tax forecast estimates what to set aside, using your own rate.
And home-office allocation reads your household rent and utilities, then proposes a business share — a proposal, not a filing.
Anything you disagree with, dismiss. It stays dismissed even as the numbers underneath keep changing.
When a month is done, close it. That freezes its totals — no edits, no imports, no accidental changes to a number you've already reported.
But before it freezes anything, it checks whether the number is worth trusting. Red is a blocker: entries with no category, or possible duplicates.
Amber is a warning — missing receipts, no bank statement imported, earlier months still open. Worth a look, but it won't stop you.
Every finding links to its own fix. Show these entries filters the ledger to the uncategorised ones; Show what's missing opens Insights.
Re-check re-runs the checks against the ledger as it is right now, and tells you the new verdict without leaving the page.
If a blocker is genuinely fine, Close anyway records on the audit trail exactly which blockers you closed over. Nothing is hidden.
Closed months show here with the option to reopen if something genuinely needs correcting.
It's record-keeping, not filing. Your accountant still files — this just means the ground stops moving under them.
At the end of the quarter, everything comes out in the formats an accountant actually wants.
A QuickBooks-ready CSV. A full Excel pack with profit and loss, income by service line, depreciation, and a document index.
Or a print view for a PDF. And the pack can be emailed to your accountant automatically, every quarter, without you remembering.
Same numbers as the screen, laid out for someone who's never seen this software.
Big purchases aren't expenses — they're assets that depreciate over years. Force plates, camera rigs, a turf build-out.
Record it once with its in-service date and useful life, and the depreciation schedule writes itself into the accountant pack.
Most of this runs without you. Income posts nightly. Receipts arrive hourly from your inbox. Payouts and fees sync daily.
A watchdog emails you if a receipt is missing for too long, and the quarterly pack goes to your accountant on schedule.
What's left for you is the judgement: categorise what's ambiguous, write down why, and confirm what the AI proposes.
And if you forget how any of this works, How to use is a written walkthrough of every screen, with an FAQ.
Same screens you've just seen, in the order you'd actually use them.
That's the AI Bookkeeper.
The same spend recorded twice is the classic bookkeeping error — a receipt you photographed, and the same charge arriving later on your bank statement.
Find duplicates pairs every two entries with the same amount and direction inside a week of each other.
Then AI judges each pair: is this really one transaction recorded twice, or two genuinely separate charges that happen to match?
Pairs that look like real duplicates are listed for review. Delete removes one side; Not a duplicate keeps both and hides the pair from every future scan.
Pairs the AI cleared are grouped below, collapsed, with one button to dismiss all of them — because the monthly close counts them until you do.
